title: Demonstrative Pronouns (Asmāʾ al-Ishārah)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 10; Ryding Ch. 13)
objectives: Distinguish near demonstratives (هٰذَا, هٰذِهِ, هٰؤُلَاءِ) from distant demonstratives (ذٰلِكَ, تِلْكَ, أُولٰئِكَ).
Differentiate a demonstrative noun phrase (هٰذَا الكِتَابُ 'this book') from a complete nominal clause (هٰذَا كِتَابٌ 'this is a book').
Apply non-human plural agreement (هٰذِهِ / تِلْكَ) to broken plurals of objects.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 2: How does definiteness distinguish a noun phrase from a complete nominal sentence?

sections.heading: Near and Distant Demonstratives
sections.body: Arabic demonstratives distinguish proximity (near: 'this/these'; distant: 'that/those') and agree in gender and number. Singular and plural demonstratives are invariable (mabnī), while dual demonstratives inflect for case (-āni / -ayni).

sections.label: Demonstrative Phrase vs. Clause
sections.summary: When a demonstrative is followed by a noun WITH أَلْ (هٰذَا الكِتَابُ), the two form a single noun phrase ('this book'), NOT a complete sentence. When followed by an INDEFINITE noun (هٰذَا كِتَابٌ), they form a complete equational sentence ('This is a book.').

sections.irab: هٰذَا: اسْمُ إِشَارَةٍ مَبْنِيٌّ فِي مَحَلِّ رَفْعٍ مُبْتَدَأٌ | الكِتَابُ: بَدَلٌ مَرْفُوعٌ | مُفِيدٌ: خَبَرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ
sections.notes: هٰذَا الكِتَابُ is only the subject phrase ('this book'); the indefinite word مُفِيدٌ completes the sentence as the predicate.

sections.heading: Demonstratives with Iḍāfah
sections.body: If the noun is already definite by iḍāfah (e.g., 'this book of the student'), the demonstrative follows the entire construct: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ هٰذَا.
